bib.title: ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence

legacy_report:
SOURCE: ClashEval: Quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence. Kevin Wu*, Eric Wu*, James Zou (Stanford). NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks track (arXiv:2404.10198v3, 7 Feb 2025).

COVERAGE: All 40,129 chars read, including the appendix (Tables 4-7, Figures 5-6 captions) and the reference list, which I skimmed. Figures 2-4 and 6 are images, so I read only their captions, not the plotted values. No extraction faults.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Models adopt wrong retrieved content over 60% of the time when their own prior was right (headline figure).
  number: 60%
  setup: 1,294 questions, 6 domains, perturbed context. Abstract and Discussion say GPT-4o. Table 2 gives 0.608 for the prior-correct case.
  quote: "LLMs are susceptible to adopting incorrect retrieved content, overriding their own correct prior knowledge over 60% of the time." / "even the most advanced LLMs like GPT-4o exhibit a strong context bias, overriding their own correct prior knowledge over 60% of the time"
  where: abstract; Discussion (p.9)
- Claim: The headline 60% does not match Table 4. Table 4 gives GPT-4o a context bias of 0.304, and the paper never explains the gap.
  number: 0.304 (Table 4) vs 0.608 (Table 2)
  setup: Table 2 is a subset (only prior or only context correct) and includes a "Neither" category. Table 4's definition is P(wrong | c wrong and r(q) right).
  quote: "GPT-4o 0.304 (0.287, 0.321) 0.021 (0.013, 0.028) 0.615 (0.594, 0.633)" / "Context 0.608 (0.571, 0.643) 0.903 (0.881, 0.923)"
  where: Table 4 (appendix); Table 2 (p.6)
- Claim: Claude Opus is best on all three metrics. Llama-3 and GPT-3.5 are near random at choosing between prior and context.
  number: Opus accuracy 74.3%, context bias 15.7%, prior bias 2.1%
  setup: 6 models, standard prompt, k=1 document
  quote: "the top performing model on all three metrics is Claude Opus, with an accuracy of 74.3%, a context bias of 15.7%, and a prior bias of 2.1%"
  where: §4.1
- Claim: The more the context deviates from truth, the less likely the model is to adopt it.
  number: Opus adheres to incorrect context 30% less than GPT-4o at the same deviation
  setup: Linear fit over numeric multipliers (0.1x to 10x), year shifts of ±100, and categorical levels (slight, significant, comical). Fit on three models in Fig 3.
  quote: "Claude Opus adheres to incorrect contextual information 30% less than GPT-4o for the same degrees of modification."
  where: §4.3, Fig 3
- Claim: The more confident the model is in its prior (token probability), the less it prefers the context.
  number: slopes -0.1 to -0.45. A slope of -0.45 means a 4.5% drop in context preference per 10% rise in prior probability.
  setup: Models that expose logprobs (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3). 10 equal probability bins. Dates are the most susceptible domain, News the most robust.
  quote: "a slope of -0.45, for instance, can be interpreted as expecting a 4.5% decrease in the likelihood of the LLM preferring the contextual information for every 10% increase in the probability of the model's prior response."
  where: §4.4
- Claim: Comparing the prior and contextual answers' token-probability percentiles reduces context bias. It also raises prior bias.
  number: GPT-4o accuracy 0.615 to 0.754, context bias 0.304 to 0.107, prior bias 0.021 to 0.085. Random baseline at 8.5% prior bias gets 57.5% accuracy against the method's 75.4%.
  setup: GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 and Llama-3 only. Raw correction: 0.693 accuracy for GPT-4o. The calibration step is needed because context-given probabilities are "extremely right-tailed" and prior probabilities "nearly uniform".
  quote: "improves all models' overall accuracy by 14% and context bias by 20%. At the same time, this introduces more prior bias, from 2% to 8.5%."
  where: §4.4.1, Table 3
- Claim: Adding documents lowers accuracy and raises the "neither" rate, but reduces context bias.
  number: Opus accuracy 0.939 (k=1) to 0.843 (k=5). GPT-4o 0.941 to 0.922. Opus prior-correct/context-chosen 0.287 to 0.237. Opus context-correct/neither 0.057 to 0.155.
  setup: GPT-4o and Opus; 4 extra documents by embedding cosine similarity. Extra documents are not described as correct or perturbed.
  quote: "adding more contextual documents lowers overall model accuracy and increases the rate of responses that are neither the prior nor the context"
  where: §4.2, Tables 6-7
- Claim: Prompt wording shifts the balance. The strict prompt enforces literal adherence to the context and the loose prompt lets the model judge. The loose prompt gives lower, steeper context-preference curves.
  number: none
  setup: GPT-4 only, one figure, no table
  quote: "We observe lower and steeper drops in context preference with the loose vs strict prompts, suggesting that prompt wording plays a significant factor in controlling context preference."
  where: Fig 6 caption (appendix)
- Claim: Bigger or more capable does not mean better for RAG. GPT-4o has more context bias than smaller models.
  number: GPT-4o 0.304, Sonnet 0.201, Gemini 1.5 0.245, Llama-3 0.264
  setup: Table 4
  quote: "While GPT-4o achieves state-of-the-art results on general-purpose tasks, it exhibits higher context bias compared to smaller models like Claude Sonnet."
  where: Discussion
- Claim: Accuracy with no context is very low on out-of-distribution News and much higher with correct context.
  number: GPT-4o News 0.0882 without context, 0.971 with correct context
  setup: Table 5, per-domain
  quote: "News 0.0882 0.971 0.469"
  where: Table 5
- Claim: Dataset size and perturbations.
  number: 1,294 questions. Numeric domains use multipliers 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 10.0.
  quote: "our dataset consists of 1,294 total questions across 6 different domains"; "ten modifications that act as multipliers on the original value: 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 10.0"
  where: §3.1, §3.3

AUDIT of note lines 329 (the passage citing arXiv 2404.10198)
- Dosage example "20 µg; context 30 answers 30; context 100 falls back to 20": I could not verify this in the paper text. The paper's text has no 20/30/100 example. The only drug example is the oxybutynin question in Table 1, and Fig 2 is an image. The note attributes it to Raieli's summary, so keep that attribution. Do not present it as the paper's own numbers. The 0.1x-10x multiplier design is consistent with it. Check Fig 2 before using it.
- "Further the context departs, the more the model trusts itself": supported (§4.3, Fig 3). It holds on average over a fitted linear trend, not as a step function, and it comes from a graded perturbation, not a single case.
- "Larger models do so more than smaller ones": not supported by this paper. No model sizes are compared, and the paper says the opposite for GPT-4o versus smaller models. It ties the trend to benchmark strength: stronger ClashEval models have a lower intercept and a more negative slope. Claude Opus (best) versus GPT-4o is a 30% difference. Reword to "stronger models on ClashEval resist more", or drop it.
- Strict, loose and standard prompts: supported in direction by the Fig 6 caption. The paper's own plot shows only strict and loose, on GPT-4, and says nothing about "standard" in the figure. The text says results are "in 6", and "standard" is the default template.
- Missing from the note: the headline 60%+ (with the Table 2 versus Table 4 caveat), the 74.3% best accuracy, the token-probability correction results, and the multi-document result.

LIMITS (authors' own)
- Domain coverage is limited.
- Questions are fact-based only, with no multi-step reasoning or synthesis.
- The dataset has an enriched rate of contextual errors, so "the reported metrics are not meant to represent bias rates in the wild".
- The probability method works only for models that expose logprobs.
- Misuse risk is noted.
- Single-document focus (the multi-document result is secondary).
- Not stated by the authors: only 2024 models were tested (GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama-3 8B, Claude Opus/Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Flash), so they have dated. The perturbed documents were partly LLM-generated by GPT-4o, and the questions and filtering were also GPT-4o-made.
- Inconsistency: the text says "Llama-3-7B-Instruct" while the contributions list says "Llama-3-8b-instruct".

BUILDS ON: Longpre et al. 2021 (entity substitution, a strong preference for training data; notation and the pretrain-on-substituted-facts idea); Xie et al. 2023 (susceptibility depends on framing; notation); Xiang et al. 2024 (ensembling isolated answers across documents); Chen et al. 2024 (RAG benchmark, noise and counterfactual robustness); Es et al. 2023 and Saad-Falcon et al. 2023 (RAG evaluation); Mitchell et al. 2023 and Zhao et al. 2024 (log probabilities as confidence); Levy et al. 2024 (longer contexts hurt).

CODE: none in the paper (data and prompts are at github.com/kevinwu23/StanfordClashEval).

FIGURES (captions only; images not viewed)
- Fig 1 (p.2): schematic of the pipeline: ask the question with and without the document, perturb the document, compare. Fastest way to see the design.
- Fig 3 (p.7): context preference falls as deviation from the reference rises.
- Fig 4 (p.8): context preference falls as prior token probability rises, per domain, with slopes.
- Fig 6 (appendix): strict versus loose prompt curves. This is what the note's prompt-strength claim rests on.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Figure 2 contents were not read, which matters for checking the dosage example. The Table 2 versus Table 4 discrepancy and the Llama-3 size inconsistency are noted above.
